{{Short description|Mathematical concept in graph theory}}
[[File:Efficient dominating set.svg|thumb|upright=0.8|The two darker vertices at the top form an '''efficient dominating set''' of the graph. Each vertex of the graph is [[dominating set|dominated]] by '''exactly one''' vertex in this set (colored by which one dominates it), including the vertices of the set, each of which dominates itself.]]

In [[graph theory]], an '''efficient dominating set''' (also called an '''e.d. set''' or '''independent perfect dominating set'''<ref name="Bange1988">{{cite conference |last1=Bange |first1=D.W. |last2=Barkauskas |first2=A.E. |last3=Slater |first3=P.J. |title=Efficient dominating sets in graphs |book-title=Applications of Discrete Mathematics |year=1988 |pages=189–199 |publisher=SIAM |location=Philadelphia}}</ref>) is a [[dominating set]] with the additional property that every [[vertex (graph theory)|vertex]] in the [[graph (discrete mathematics)|graph]] is dominated by exactly one vertex in the set.<ref name="Brandstadt2012">{{cite conference |last1=Brandstädt |first1=Andreas |last2=Leitert |first2=Arne |last3=Rautenbach |first3=Dieter |title=Efficient Dominating and Edge Dominating Sets for Graphs and Hypergraphs |book-title=Algorithms and Computation |series=Lecture Notes in Computer Science |volume=7676 |year=2012 |pages=267–277 |publisher=Springer |location=Berlin, Heidelberg |doi=10.1007/978-3-642-35261-4_30 |isbn=978-3-642-35261-4 |arxiv=1207.0953}}</ref>

The '''efficient domination problem''' (ED problem) asks whether a given graph contains an efficient dominating set. The problem is [[NP-complete]] for general graphs<ref name="Brandstadt2012" /> and remains NP-complete even when restricted to [[planar graph|3-regular planar graphs]].<ref name="Livingston1990">{{cite journal |last1=Livingston |first1=Marilynn |last2=Stout |first2=Quentin F. |title=Perfect dominating sets |journal=Congressus Numerantium |volume=79 |year=1990 |pages=187–203 |url=https://web.eecs.umich.edu/~qstout/pap/BR90pds.pdf}}</ref>

== Definition ==
A vertex <math>v</math> in a graph '''dominates''' itself and all its neighbors, that is, every vertex <math>u</math> such that <math>u = v</math> or <math>uv \in E</math>. A [[dominating set]] <math>D</math> is a set of vertices such that every vertex in the graph is dominated by at least one vertex in <math>D</math>. An ''efficient'' dominating set strengthens this condition by requiring that every vertex is dominated by '''exactly one''' vertex in <math>D</math>.<ref name="Brandstadt2012" />

More formally, a vertex set <math>D \subseteq V</math> in a graph <math>G = (V,E)</math> is an efficient dominating set if for every vertex <math>v \in V</math>, there is exactly one <math>d \in D</math> such that <math>v</math> is in the [[Neighbourhood (graph theory)|closed neighborhood]] <math>N_G[d]</math> of <math>d</math>.<ref name="Brandstadt2012" />

An equivalent characterization is that the closed neighborhoods <math>{N_G[d] : d \in D}</math> form a [[Partition of a set|partition]] of the vertex set <math>V</math>.<ref name="Livingston1990" />

Every efficient dominating set is necessarily a [[minimum dominating set]], since the closed neighborhoods partition the vertex set.<ref name="Livingston1990" /> However, not every minimum dominating set is efficient.

== Complexity ==
The efficient domination problem is [[NP-complete]] for several graph classes, including [[bipartite graph]]s, [[chordal graph]]s, and [[chordal bipartite graph]]s<ref name="Brandstadt2012" />. The problem remains NP-complete even when restricted to 3-regular planar graphs.<ref name="Livingston1990" />

However, the problem can be solved in [[polynomial time]] for certain restricted graph classes:<ref name="Brandstadt2012" /><ref name="Livingston1990" />

*[[Dually chordal graph]]s can be solved in [[linear time]]
*[[AT-free graph]]s can be solved in polynomial time
*[[Interval graph|Interval bigraphs]] can be solved in polynomial time
*[[Tree (graph theory)|Trees]] can be solved in linear time

== Examples ==

[[Sierpiński graph]]s <math>S(n,k)</math> provide notable examples of graphs with efficient dominating sets. These graphs possess essentially unique efficient dominating sets for all parameters <math>n</math> and <math>k</math>.<ref name="Klavzar2002">{{cite journal |last1=Klavžar |first1=Sandi |last2=Milutinović |first2=Uroš |last3=Petr |first3=Ciril |title=1-perfect codes in Sierpiński graphs |journal=Bulletin of the Australian Mathematical Society |volume=66 |issue=3 |year=2002 |pages=369–384 |doi=10.1017/S0004972700040235|doi-access=free }}</ref><ref name="Klavzar2008">{{cite journal |last=Klavžar |first=Sandi |title=Coloring Sierpiński graphs and Sierpiński gasket graphs |journal=Taiwanese Journal of Mathematics |volume=12 |issue=2 |year=2008 |pages=513–522 |doi=10.11650/twjm/1500574171 |jstor=43833928}}</ref>

The closely related [[Hanoi graph|Sierpiński gasket graphs]] <math>S_n</math>, which arise from iterations leading to the [[Sierpiński triangle|Sierpiński gasket]], have a much more restrictive structure: they contain an efficient dominating set if and only if <math>n = 1</math> or <math>n = 3</math>.<ref name="Klavzar2008" />

[[Circulant graph]]s provide another well-studied class for efficient dominating sets. A circulant graph <math>\text{Cay}(\mathbb{Z}_n, S)</math> is a [[Cayley graph]] on the [[cyclic group]] <math>\mathbb{Z}_n</math> with connection set <math>S</math>, where <math>S = -S</math> and <math>0 \notin S</math>. Such a graph has vertices <math>\{0, 1, \ldots, n-1\}</math> with edges connecting vertices whose difference lies in <math>S</math>.<ref name="Deng2017">{{cite journal |last1=Deng |first1=Yun-Ping |last2=Sun |first2=Yu-Qin |last3=Liu |first3=Qiong |last4=Wang |first4=Hai-Chao |title=Efficient dominating sets in circulant graphs |journal=Discrete Mathematics |volume=340 |issue=7 |year=2017 |pages=1503–1507 |doi=10.1016/j.disc.2017.02.014 |issn=0012-365X}}</ref>

For a circulant graph <math>\text{Cay}(\mathbb{Z}_n, S)</math> to admit an efficient dominating set <math>D</math>, a necessary condition is <math>n = |S_0| \cdot |D|</math>, where <math>S_0 = S \cup \{0\}</math>.<ref name="Deng2017" />

For connected non-complete circulant graphs of degree <math>|S| = p - 1</math> where <math>p</math> is prime, an efficient dominating set exists if and only if <math>s - s' \not\equiv 0 \pmod{p}</math> for any distinct <math>s, s' \in S_0</math>. When this condition holds, all efficient dominating sets are precisely the cosets <math>g + p\mathbb{Z}_n</math> for <math>g \in \mathbb{Z}_n</math>.<ref name="Deng2017" />

Similar characterizations exist for circulant graphs of degree <math>|S| = pq - 1</math> and <math>|S| = p^m - 1</math>, where <math>p, q</math> are primes and <math>m</math> is a positive integer, provided that <math>|S| + 1</math> is relatively prime to <math>\frac{n}{|S|+1}</math>.<ref name="Deng2017" />

== History and applications ==
The concept of efficient dominating sets was introduced independently by two groups of researchers. [[Norman L. Biggs|Norman Biggs]] first studied these structures in 1973 under the name '''perfect codes''' in the context of [[coding theory]] and [[distance-transitive graph]]s.<ref name="Biggs1973">{{cite journal |last=Biggs |first=Norman |title=Perfect codes in graphs |journal=Journal of Combinatorial Theory, Series B |volume=15 |issue=3 |year=1973 |pages=289–296 |doi=10.1016/0095-8956(73)90042-7 |doi-access=free}}</ref> Later, apparently unaware of Biggs's work, Bange, Barkauskas, and Slater independently defined the concept as '''efficient dominating sets''' and developed [[linear time]] algorithms for finding them in [[tree (graph theory)|trees]].<ref name="Bange1988" /><ref name="Livingston1990" />

Efficient dominating sets have applications in [[resource allocation]] problems for [[parallel computing]]. When modeling a parallel computer's processors and interconnection network as a graph, an efficient dominating set represents an optimal placement of limited resources (such as disk drives, I/O connections, or software modules) such that every processor is within distance <math>d</math> of exactly one resource unit, with neither duplication nor overlap.<ref name="Livingston1990" />

The concept has been extended to [[fuzzy graph]]s and intuitionistic fuzzy graphs, where efficient domination has been applied to [[encryption]] and [[decryption]] problems. In these applications, efficient dominating nodes serve as centers of subnetworks in the encryption scheme, and identifying the efficiently dominating set becomes the secret key for decryption.<ref name="Kumaran2023">{{cite journal |last1=Kumaran |first1=N. |last2=Meenakshi |first2=A. |last3=Mahdal |first3=M. |last4=Prakash |first4=J.U. |last5=Guras |first5=R. |title=Application of Fuzzy Network Using Efficient Domination |journal=Mathematics |volume=11 |issue=10 |year=2023 |pages=2258 |doi=10.3390/math11102258 |doi-access=free|hdl=10084/152009 |hdl-access=free }}</ref>

For [[hypercube graph]]s, a distance d efficient dominating set corresponds precisely to a '''perfect binary d-error-correcting code'''.<ref name="Livingston1990" /><ref name="Biggs1973" /> This connection links the graph-theoretic concept to [[coding theory]].

== Related problems ==
The '''efficient edge domination problem''' (EED problem) is the edge-analogue of the efficient domination problem. An '''efficient edge dominating set''' <math>M \subseteq E</math> is a set of edges such that every edge <math>e \in E</math> is intersected by exactly one edge <math>e' \in M</math>. The EED problem can be solved in linear time for [[chordal graph]]s and [[dually chordal graph]]s.<ref name="Brandstadt2012" />

A '''strong efficient dominating set''' is a variant where domination is restricted to neighbors of equal or higher degree. Formally, a set <math>S \subseteq V</math> is a strong efficient dominating set if for every <math>v \in V</math>, there is exactly one vertex in <math>S</math> that either equals <math>v</math> or is adjacent to <math>v</math> with degree at least <math>\deg(v)</math>. Unlike standard efficient dominating sets, which all have the same cardinality in a given graph, strong efficient dominating sets of the same graph may have different cardinalities.<ref name="Meena2014">{{cite journal |last1=Meena |first1=N. |last2=Subramanian |first2=A. |last3=Swaminathan |first3=V. |title=Strong efficient domination in graphs |journal=International Journal of Innovative Science, Engineering & Technology |volume=1 |issue=4 |year=2014 |pages=172–177 |issn=2348-7968 |url=https://www.ijiset.com/v1s4/IJISET_V1_I4_22.pdf}}</ref>

The concept extends naturally to '''distance d perfect dominating sets''' (or '''distance d PDS'''). A vertex <math>v</math> '''d-dominates''' a vertex <math>u</math> if the distance between them is at most <math>d</math>. A set <math>D</math> is a distance d perfect dominating set if every vertex in the graph is d-dominated by exactly one vertex in <math>D</math>.<ref name="Livingston1990" />

The concept also extends to [[hypergraph]]s, where similar complexity results have been established.<ref name="Brandstadt2012" />
